denomProfiles/waldensian/tagline: Medieval movement of lay preachers that became Italy's historic Reformed church.
denomProfiles/waldensian/coreDoctrines/0: Scripture as the sole rule of faith, read in the vernacular.
denomProfiles/waldensian/coreDoctrines/1: Reformed theology, adopted at the Synod of Chanforan in 1532.
denomProfiles/waldensian/coreDoctrines/3: Two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper.
denomProfiles/waldensian/coreDoctrines/4: Historically, rejection of purgatory, prayers for the dead and oath-taking.
denomProfiles/waldensian/focuses/1: Social service, funded in part by Italy's "eight per thousand" tax scheme.
denomProfiles/waldensian/focuses/2: Ecumenism and dialogue, including at the Agape centre (founded 1947).
denomProfiles/waldensian/focuses/3: Theological education at the Waldensian Faculty of Theology in Rome.
denomProfiles/waldensian/focuses/4: Progressive ethics, including the blessing of same-sex unions (Synod of 2010).
denomProfiles/waldensian/practices/1: Infant baptism and the Lord's Supper.
denomProfiles/waldensian/practices/2: An annual synod each August at Torre Pellice.
denomProfiles/waldensian/influenced/0/te: The Waldensians funded this first French Protestant Bible.
denomProfiles/waldensian/influenced/1/te: United with Italian Methodists in 1975 in the Union of Methodist and Waldensian Churches.
denomProfiles/waldensian/influenced/2/te: The Piedmont massacre of 1655 inspired Milton's sonnet "On the Late Massacre in Piedmont".
denomProfiles/waldensian/keyFigures/0/ro: Merchant who founded the movement c. 1173.
denomProfiles/waldensian/keyFigures/1/ro: Pastor who led the "Glorious Return" to the valleys in 1689.
denomProfiles/waldensian/keyFigures/2/ro: Founder of the Agape ecumenical centre and the Riesi mission.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/tagline: Bohemian reform from Jan Hus to the Unity of the Brethren.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/coreDoctr: Scripture as the supreme authority, above popes and councils.
Communion in both kinds (bread and wine) for the laity.
The Four Articles of Prague (1420): free preaching, the cup for the laity, clerical poverty and punishment of public sin.
For the Unity of the Brethren, faith expressed in a disciplined, peaceable common life.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/focuses/0: Reform of the clergy and church.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/focuses/1: Vernacular preaching and Bible translation, culminating in the Kralice Bible (1579–93).
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/focuses/3: Education, championed by Jan Amos Comenius.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/practices: The Unity's own episcopal ministry from 1467.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/influence: Luther declared in 1520 that "we are all Hussites" without knowing it.
Renewed at Herrnhut in 1727 by descendants of the Unity of the Brethren.
Hus and the Hussites became symbols of the modern Czech nation; the Czechoslovak Hussite Church was founded in 1920.
denomProfiles/hussite-moravian/keyFigure: Reformer burned at the Council of Constance in 1415.
Lay thinker whose ideas shaped the Unity.
Educator and the last bishop of the old Unity.
denomProfiles/african-initiated-churches: Churches founded and led by Africans, uniting the Bible with African life.
Faith in the Triune God and Christ, read through the Bible, especially the Old Testament and the Gospels.
The Holy Spirit's power for healing, prophecy and protection from evil.
Revelation through prophet-founders, dreams and visions in many churches.
Salvation understood holistically, including health, fertility and well-being.
Healing through prayer, holy water and other blessed objects.
Protection from witchcraft and evil spirits.
African leadership and dignity, against colonial and mission control.
Community life, pilgrimage and holy places.
Baptism, often by immersion in rivers or the sea.
White robes or uniforms, removal of shoes and food taboos in many churches.
Leadership by prophets, bishops and founders' families.
Pilgrimage to holy cities such as Moria, Nkamba and Ekuphakameni.
Dancing, drumming and African hymnody in worship.
African Pentecostalism
Later Pentecostal churches often grew among former members.
African theology
Theologians such as Kwame Bediako drew on them for a genuinely African Christianity.
African diaspora churches
AICs became established in Britain, Europe and North America.
Mangena Mokone
Founder of the Ethiopian Church (1892).
William Wade Harris
Liberian prophet whose 1913–15 mission founded the Harrist churches.
Simon Kimbangu
Congolese prophet-healer.
Isaiah Shembe
Founder of the Nazareth Baptist Church (1910).
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/tag: Unregistered Chinese Protestant churches that grew under persecution.
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/cor: Evangelical faith with Scripture as supreme authority.
Separation of church from state control, rejecting the Three-Self Patriotic Movement.
A theology of the cross: suffering for Christ as normal for believers.
In rural networks, Pentecostal-type healing and miracles; in many urban churches, Reformed theology.
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/foc: Evangelism by itinerant preachers, including the "Back to Jerusalem" vision.
Faithfulness under pressure from the authorities.
Training of leaders in secret seminaries.
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/pra: Worship in homes, rented offices and other unregistered spaces.
Believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper.
Singing of indigenous songs such as Lü Xiaomin's Canaan Hymns.
Large networks in the countryside and independent churches in cities.
Women are leading evangelists and preachers, especially in rural networks.
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/inf: House church emigrants and theology influence overseas Chinese churches.
Its vision of mission towards the Middle East won wide support abroad.
denomProfiles/chinese-house-churches/key: Independent Beijing pastor imprisoned 1955–1979 for refusing to join the TSPM.
Founder of the Little Flock, imprisoned from 1952.
Guangzhou house church pastor imprisoned for over 20 years.
Pastor of Early Rain Covenant Church, Chengdu, sentenced to nine years in 2019.
denomProfiles/quaker/tagline: Friends who wait in silence on the Inward Light and witness for peace.
denomProfiles/quaker/coreDoctrines/0: The Inward Light of Christ, given to every person.
denomProfiles/quaker/coreDoctrines/1: Direct revelation of Christ through the Spirit, tested against Scripture and the gathered meeting.
denomProfiles/quaker/coreDoctrines/2: The priesthood of all believers, without ordained clergy.
denomProfiles/quaker/coreDoctrines/3: Inward baptism and communion rather than outward rites.
denomProfiles/quaker/coreDoctrines/4: Testimonies of peace, simplicity, integrity, equality and community.
denomProfiles/quaker/focuses/1: Social reform, including abolition of slavery and prison reform.
denomProfiles/quaker/focuses/2: Service and relief, recognised by the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947.
denomProfiles/quaker/focuses/3: Equality of women and men in ministry from the movement's beginning.
denomProfiles/quaker/practices/0: Unprogrammed meetings for worship in silence, broken by spoken ministry.
denomProfiles/quaker/practices/1: Programmed and evangelical churches with pastors, hymns and sermons, especially in Kenya and the US.
denomProfiles/quaker/practices/2: Meetings for worship for business that seek unity rather than vote.
denomProfiles/quaker/influenced/0/text: The Shakers grew from the "Shaking Quakers" of north-west England.
denomProfiles/quaker/influenced/1/text: From the Germantown protest of 1688 to John Woolman, Quakers led opposition to slavery.
denomProfiles/quaker/influenced/2/text: William Penn's colony pioneered religious freedom.
denomProfiles/quaker/influenced/3/text: The American Friends Service Committee and Friends Service Council inspired modern relief work.
denomProfiles/quaker/keyFigures/0/role: Founder and author of the Journal.
denomProfiles/quaker/keyFigures/1/role: Mother of Quakerism, of Swarthmoor Hall.
denomProfiles/quaker/keyFigures/2/role: Author of the Apology for the True Christian Divinity (1676).
denomProfiles/quaker/members/note: Friends World Committee for Consultation count of Quakers worldwide.
denomProfiles/quaker/inIndia: British Friends began mission work at Hoshangabad in present-day Madhya Pradesh in the 1870s, and American Friends worked in Bundelkhand from the 1890s; small meetings, schools and service projects survive there and in Delhi.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/tagline: Renewed Unity of the Brethren known for heart religion and pioneering missions.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/coreDoctri: Scripture as the sole standard of doctrine, with the Ground of the Unity (1957).
Heart religion: a personal relationship with the crucified Christ.
Respect for the ecumenical creeds and the Augsburg Confession, without elaborate systems.
"In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things love."
denomProfiles/moravian-church/focuses/0: World mission, from the Caribbean and Greenland (1732–33) to Africa and Asia.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/focuses/3: Prayer, including the 24-hour prayer watch begun in 1727.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/practices/: Lovefeasts with shared bread and coffee or tea.
Easter sunrise services in God's Acre burial grounds.
Infant baptism, confirmation and Holy Communion.
Bishops in a succession claimed from 1467, within synodal government; women ordained in most provinces.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/influenced: John Wesley met Moravians in Georgia and London, and his Aldersgate conversion (1738) came through the Fetter Lane Society.
William Carey cited Moravian example in 1792.
The theologian was educated by Moravians and called himself "a Moravian of a higher order".
denomProfiles/moravian-church/keyFigures: Patron and leader of the renewed church.
Carpenter who led the first refugees to Herrnhut.
Bishop who organised the church in North America.
denomProfiles/moravian-church/inIndia: Moravians worked at Tranquebar and in the Nicobar Islands (1760s–1803) and from 1853 in the Himalaya, at Kyelang in Lahaul and from 1885 at Leh in Ladakh, where Heinrich August Jäschke translated the Bible into Tibetan; small Moravian congregations remain in Ladakh.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/tagline: Congolese church born of Simon Kimbangu's healing ministry and colonial persecution.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/coreDoc: Faith in God, Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, with the Bible as Scripture.
Simon Kimbangu as a prophet sent by God to Africa.
Later teaching identifies Kimbangu with the Comforter promised in John 14 and gives his descendants an exalted place; other Congolese Protestants have questioned this.
Non-violence and obedience to God's law.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/focuses: Moral discipline: no alcohol, tobacco, pork, polygamy or violence.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/practic: Baptism by laying on of hands, without water.
Holy Communion with bread and drink made from local produce (since 1971).
Removal of shoes on holy ground at Nkamba.
Leadership by a spiritual head from Kimbangu's family.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/influen: Kimbangu became a symbol of resistance to Belgian colonial rule.
It became a model for independent churches and joined the WCC in 1969.
denomProfiles/kimbanguist-church/keyFigu: Prophet whose 1921 healing ministry began the church (d. 1951).
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/tagl: Southern Africa's largest church, of healing, uniforms and the Easter pilgrimage to Moria.
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/core: Faith in the Triune God and Jesus Christ, with Scripture as read by the bishop.
Healing through the power of the Holy Spirit.
Obedience to the bishop as the leader appointed by God.
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/focu: Healing through prayer, blessed water, tea, needles and cords.
Moral discipline: no alcohol, tobacco or pork.
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/prac: Easter pilgrimage to Zion City Moria near Polokwane, drawing over a million people.
Badges with a star (ZCC) or dove (St Engenas ZCC) and khaki or green uniforms.
The men's mokhukhu dance in worship.
Hereditary leadership by the Lekganyane family; women are not ordained.
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/infl: Leaders from P. W. Botha (1985) to Nelson Mandela (1992) addressed the Easter gathering.
It is the largest of the many Zionist churches.
denomProfiles/zion-christian-church/keyF: His son, leader of the ZCC (star) after the 1949 split (d. 1967).
